senses: A community of the Knights Templar, or the physical buildings or estate of such a community.
ety: From Medieval Latin praeceptoria, noun use of the feminine of praeceptorius (“commanding”), ultimately from praeceptor + -ius. Equivalent to preceptor + -y.

senses: The state or quality of being believable.
A citrus fruit that is a cross between a tangerine and a pomelo or a grapefruit.
A red-orange colour, like that of a tangelo.
Not marriageable, unsuitable for marriage.
That cannot be reconciled, inconsistent.
examples: You have always had a little way of alluding to her as an unmarriageable girl.
He had a way of pronouncing the word "miss" that made it an epithet, a sneer at her unmarried and unmarriageable state.
A link was wanting between two craving parts of nature, and he was hurled into being as the bridge over that yawning need, the mediator betwixt two else unmarriageable facts.

senses: A gem variety of microcline feldspar, varying from bright verdigris green to a bluish green.
ety: From Amazon + -ite; the gem does not actually come from the Amazon, but it was confused with an unrelated green stone that does.

senses: Enthusiasm for films and the cinema.
examples: Perhaps it is not cinema that has ended but only cinephilia—the name of the very specific kind of love that cinema inspired. Each art breeds its fanatics.
Loudly and proudly declaring your love of Letterboxd has become a way of demonstrating your superior cinephilia.

senses: A hot relish made from chili peppers and other ingredients.
ety: Borrowed, either directly or via Afrikaans sambal, from Malay sambal, from Javanese ꦱꦩ꧀ꦧꦼꦭ꧀ (sambel).

senses: Psychrolutes marcidus, a fish that inhabits the deep waters off the coasts of the Australian mainland and Tasmania.
ety: From blob + fish, from its shape.

senses: A werewolf or werewolf-like creature said to inhabit the swamps in Louisiana (and sometimes French-Canadian) folklore.
To excavate using such equipment.
Any of several plants of the tribe Cassieae, especially those of the genera Cassia and Senna, whose leaves and pods are used as a purgative and laxative.
The dried leaves or pods of these plants (especially of Senna alexandrina, syn. Cassia angustifolia or Cassia acutifolia), used medicinally.
Synonym of fluorite.
A wing feather from a female ostrich.
ety: From Latin fēmina (“woman”), perhaps via Italian femmina. Doublet of feme, femme, and hembra.
examples: The usual kinds of ostrich feathers known to the trade come into the Tripoli market. These are whites, blacks, feminas, byocks, spadonas, boos, drabs and floss.
The feminas brought from $97.35 to $109.50, while spadones were sacrificed at from $34 to $47.45.
It is somewhat larger than the Southern bird and the plumage of young birds and also the feminas are darker.

senses: A speech made when leaving or parting company.
The act of parting company.
A word or phrase said upon leaving, such as "farewell" or "adieu".
A word or phrase used to end a letter or message.
ety: First attested in 1614; borrowed from New Latin valedictiō, from valedīcō (“to bid farewell”) + -tiō, from valē (“farewell, so long”) + dīcō (“to say”). By surface analysis, valedict + -ion.

senses: An Ancient Greek letter representing /w/: Ϝ, ϝ
ety: From di- + gamma, from its shape resembling two stacked capital gammas (Γ).

senses: A member of a militia.
the plant that is the source of pollen for cross-pollination
Growing inside another organism, e.g. of parasites or cancer tumors.
transparent or glassy
ety: From Ancient Greek ὑαλοειδής (hualoeidḗs), from ὕαλος (húalos, “glass”) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-id”).

senses: The reddish purple colour of the apéritif Dubonnet.
The principle or practice of corporate action; (in later use chiefly) specifically, a political ideology which advocates for government and social organization by collective interest groups.
A tannery, or a yard of a tannery.
To shear or shave off; shear or shave all over.
ety: From Middle English bischeren, from Old English besċieran, besċeran (“to shear, shave, cut hair, give the tonsure”), from Proto-West Germanic *biskeran (“to cut off”), equivalent to be- (“around, off, away”) + shear. Cognate with Saterland Frisian beskere, West Frisian beskeare, Dutch bescheren, German Low German bescheren, German bescheren.

senses: A type of soy sauce made without wheat, having a rich flavor.
An alderman or alderwoman.
examples: Almost immediately, city alders contacted the campaign to negotiate an ordinance.
Chicago's mayor Edward Kennelly, the city alders, and many white Chicagoans opposed this siting plan.
After three years as Ward 1 alder, Sarah Eidelson ’12 will leave city government at the end of the year.

senses: The top step of the crepidoma, i.e. the platform upon which the superstructure of the building is erected.
ety: Borrowed from Latin stylobata, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek στυλοβάτης (stulobátēs), from στῦλος (stûlos, “pillar”) + βαίνω (baínō, “to go, to walk”).

senses: A member at one end of a range or series made up of similar members.
A hot rod enthusiast.
Less than usually intense
Abutting or near the kidneys.
Full of excitement or adrenaline.
ety: From ad- (“near”) + renal (“pertaining to the kidneys”), from Latin rēn (“kidney”).

senses: Tending to self-denial; ascetic.
Any of two or more atomic nuclei with the same mass number and atomic number but with different radioactive properties.
Of, or resembling wood; woody.
ety: From Latin ligneus; compare Latin lignōsus; equivalent to lign- + -eous.

senses: An official who visits agricultural lands and maintains records of their ownership and tilling.
ety: Borrowed from Urdu پَٹْوَاری (paṭvārī) / Hindi पाटवारी (pāṭvārī) or Bengali পাটোয়ারি (paṭōẇari, “rent collector”).

senses: To put an end to; to do away with.
To block a process or function.
Of poor or dubious quality, shoddy, unreliable; deviously dishonest, fraudulent.
ety: From 1970s; possibly from dialectal English shonk (“smart”).
examples: He might be a dole-bludger, a gambler and have the shonkiest tattoo in the world on his arm, but he'll agree to almost anything.
That′s why it is infuriating that there are still so many sharks out there who are determined to rip men off with shonky treatments that simply don′t work.
Marred by shonky direction and factual errors, the film did nothing to enhance Kathner′s already poor reputation.

senses: A kind of heat-resistant borosilicate glass, made by mixing a high concentration of boron oxides into the molten glass to reduce its thermal expansion coefficient.
Any borosilicate glass.
Any glass capable of withstanding high temperatures, such as tempered glass suitable for cooking.
examples: This steel tube slips into the pyrex glass focus tube, which is jacketed by a vacuum
There is half of a yesteryear's tin of baked beans in a pyrex bowl

I tiptoed into the kitchen, turned on the fluorescent light over the stove, and peered into the oven. It was still warm, though the gas had been turned off. My dinner was there, in a pyrex dish with a cover.

senses: A horizontal line over the top of some of the terms in an expression, indicating that that part of the calculation is to be done before other parts (in modern mathematical notation confined to use in radicals: √).
The horizontal line between the numerator and denominator in a fraction.
A horizontal line placed over one or more digits of a decimal expansion to indicate that those digits repeat indefinitely (the repetend).
A symbol in the shape of an elongated letter "S" (∫) or pair of hooks (⌠⌡) drawn on plans to join non-contiguous sections of land that are to be treated as a single parcel.
ety: From Latin vinculum (“bond, link”), from vinciō (“bind, fetter, tie”) + -ulum.

senses: Withania somnifera, a stout shrub that produces red berry-like fruit, native to India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka.
ety: Borrowed from Sanskrit अश्वगन्धा (aśvagandhā, literally “horse’s smell”).

senses: A (male) leader; an important (male) person.
A person who purports to stay aloof from party politics.
One who switches from supporting one political party to another, especially for personal benefit.
A foolish person.
ety: The noun is borrowed from Massachusett mugquomp, mummugquomp (“war leader”). Folk etymology reinterpreted it as referring to a person who sat on the fence with their mug (“face”) on one side and wump (“rump”) on the other, which influenced political cartoons during the 1884 United States presidential election. The verb is derived from the noun.
